The methodology enhances the loading process by applying advanced algorithms and metaheuristics to identify optimal locations for each Stock Keeping Unit (SKU). One of the central issues we address in this study is the Container Loading Problem (CLP), an NP-Hard problem that has persisted for many years. The approach undertaken here is twofold: firstly, to maximize space utilization, thereby reducing the wastage of slots, and second ly, to strategically assign locations for each SKU based on the overall order quantity. This two -step methodology enables us to calculate the total number of PODs (Portable On Demand storage units) required for efficient operations. This research was condu cted by incorporating real -world observations and adjusting empirical data to simulate a practical context for our experiment. This experiment ’s constraints also reflect real -world limitations, including the direction of rotation and the restriction agains t placing different SKUs in the same slot.

These factors make our study more reflective of the challenges faced in warehouse environments. This research demonstrates that our method effectively identifies the accurate number of PODs required to fulfill the order requirements, thus helping warehouses minimize the cost of surplus POD placements. By providing a means to a nticipate the required number of PODs accurately, our study contributes to the wider discourse on improving warehouse efficiency and decreasing operational costs.

We believe these insights and the associated strategies presented here can be a valuable resource for businesses looking to optimize their RMFS operations and achieve significant cost reductions. According to analysts, the global ecommerce share of retail sales is predicted to grow this year and reach 20.8%. By 2026, it is forecasted to increase by 5.2 percentage points to 24%, indicating significant growth in just six years [1]. Hence, conventional transportation methods are inadequate, and adopting automated and efficient means of retrieving and transporting goods is imperative .

Achieving automation in the warehouse plays a vital role in attaining optimal levels of automation and autonomy, which leads to faster, safer, and more efficient day -to-day operations. By leveraging automated processes in the warehouse, costs are reduced, and delivery times are improved, resul ting in a leaner, more scalable, and eco-friendly operation [2].

Implementing automation in order-picking is possible by utilizing the Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS), a semi-automated parts-to-picker system commonly employed in ecommerce warehouses. This system employs an automatic guided vehicle (AG V) to convey movable shelves (pods) to the designated picking stations, facilitating the automation process. Despite advancements in the implementation of this system, there are several distinct actions carried out by different entities at various phases of the robot routing problem [3], product assignment, pod storage allocation [4], layout design [5], and AGV energy consumption [6].

The task of executing RMFS is a laborious undertaking that involves numerous intricate subproblems. Without proper management, the RMFS cannot run the warehouse smoothly. Therefore, many studies have been working on RMFS [7].

Yang, Jin [8] Conducted a study that analyzed the effect of warehouse configuration on the throughput. They analyzed some factors, including lane depth, number of aisles, picking stations, and robots. Yang and Hua [9] optimize robot utilization by designing a policy for order sequencing and rack scheduling. Keung, Lee [10] focuses on the charging assignment problem. Some recent studies focus on pic k order and pod assignment, including [11, 12].

Among all problems in RMFS, one problem that also might influence the efficiency of the warehouse is the item-to-pod allocation problem. While most of the studies focus on pod allocation 2 and pod selection based on demand, very limited studies discuss the item -to-pod assignment, which also considers the dimension of the items. An optimal item assign ment to the pods might reduce the pods required to fulfill the demand. Thus, it can reduce the cost of pod investment, the size of the storage area in the warehouse, and the overall warehouse operational cost. Therefore, this study aims to improve pod utilization by optimizing the item-to-pod assignment. The item -to-pod assignment problem is similar to the three -dimensional (3D) bin -packing problem. The 3D bin packing problem, an extension of the one-dimensional and two-dimensional problems, is crucial in logistics planning. It is ubiquitous in the real world, encompassing steel, textiles, transportation, and manufacturing industries. It aims to increase the utilization rate of trucks or containers to enhance system efficiency.

In this study, the 3D bin -packing problem is applied in RMFS to reduce the extra costs caused by the need for multiple shelves due to inefficient warehouse shelf space utilization. The Bin Packing Problem (BPP) is one of the most famous problems in combinatorial optimization problems that manifest in numerous practical applications within the fields of transportation and logistics.
According to the improved typology of Wäscher, Haußner [13], BPP has been studied since the 1970s [14, 15]. However, the implementation of BPP in RMFS is still rare.

A similar problem with BPP is the container loading problem (CLP). Both BPP and CLP are categorized as NP-hard problems. Until recent years, there has been research proposing the use of deep learning to solve such problems. However, heuristic algo rithms remain the most favored by many. Hajlaoui and Jaoua [16] present a new Reinforcement Learning model for container loading. It performs well and shows that l ower training variability yields better results than high training variability.

Kurpel and Scarpin [17] offer new, effective solutions for container loading problems, considering conditions like box orientation, load stability, and separation of boxes. Zhang, Gu [18] introduces a new hybrid heuristic algorithm to address the container loading problem efficiently . Gajda, Trivella [19] introduces a new heuristic algorithm to solve a comp lex logistics problem, balancing cargo value and multiple constraints. A pod in RMFS consists of several slots.

The slots can have the same or different sizes. Maximizing the number of items stored in a slot is similar to the 3D bin packing problem. This study proposes a heuristics algorithm to design the item’s arrangement in a slot to optimize the slot’s utilization. Furthermore, because there are many different slots and pods, the next problem is which item should be stored in which slot in which pod.

This problem is a combinatorial problem. 3 Therefore, this study applies a metaheuristics approach to solve this problem. Regarding algorithm selection, we adopted GA and PSO, which have been widely used [20-23], as our methodologies. 1.2 Objectives This study aims to optimize pod utilization by maximizing the number of items stored in each slot and finding the best item -slot-pod arrangement.

This study combines heuristics and metaheuristics algorithms to find the optimal solution. T his study applies two metaheuristics algorithms: particle swarm optimization (PSO) and genetic algorithm (GA).

text: 2.2 Container loading problem The CLP is a geometric assignment challenge that entails loading a subset of rectangular items, often denoted as SKU (Stock Keeping Units), into a fixed-dimension rectangular container, such as pods. The aim is to maximize the volume of the packed boxes. The packing process has to satisfy an optimized objective function under two primary geometric feasibility prerequisites: • Every small item must be completely contained within the large object, and • There should be no overlapping among the smaller units. CLP are diverse, with various properties constituting their characteristics. They are traditionally categorized into two groups, as outlined by Wäscher and Haußner [13].

Conversely, the second group, the output maximization problem, operates under limited container space, which is insufficient for storing all boxes.
